figures.label: S1
figures.caption: Figure S1: A matrix plot showing the pairwise correlation between any of the two forma- tion parameters. The numbers inside each square represent the Pearson coefficient. The low Pearson coefficient between non identical parameters confirms that Latin hypercube sampling minimizes the parameter correlation during experiment design.

figures.label: S2
figures.caption: Figure S2: Histograms of the parameter value distribution for the first 150-cell batch. As a reference, 1C current is defined as 0.24 A for this dataset.

figures.label: S3
figures.caption: Figure S3: Histograms of the parameter value distribution for the 36 fast-formed cells in batch 2.

figures.label: S5
figures.caption: Figure S5: Baseline formation protocol, C/20 charge and discharge, 1 cycle, at 40◦C [3–5]. The three repeats of the baseline protocol correspond to sequence number 324, 325, 326.

figures.label: S6
figures.caption: Figure S6: Distribution of normalized C/20 discharge capacities immediately after forma- tion for 186 cells. Each protocol has 3 replicates and the mean capacity of each protocol is used for normalization. The cell capacity distribution is centered around 1, so the cell-to-cell variability is minimal.

figures.label: S7
figures.caption: Figure S7: Distribution of normalized cycle life for 186 cells. Each protocol has 3 repli- cates and the mean cycle life for each protocol is used for normalization. Battery aging introduces an expected increase in variability for metrics. For the majority of cells, their cycle life lies within a 10% deviation of the mean.

figures.label: S8
figures.caption: Figure S8: How the 6 formation parameters affect metrics at different stages of cycling: (1) cycle 0, after formation but before cycling aging (2) after 120 aging cycles (3) at the end of life. The plot is generated by constructing random forest models using the 6 formation parameters and extracting their importance on metrics via SHAP analysis. Darker colors in the matrix plot indicate a larger impact. The prediction errors of the models are listed in Table.S1.

figures.label: S9
figures.caption: Figure S9: Both formation temperature and formation currents positively affect cycle life. When the parameter value increases, the impact is also increasing in the positive direction as shown in the plot. During model training, the errors for training and test are: Train MAPE = 23.4% Train RMSE = 0.090 Test MAPE = 35.2% Test RMSE = 0.152. The cycle life label is normalized to be between 0 and 1 during model training.

figures.label: S10
figures.caption: Figure S10: First-cycle electrochemistry during formation for three repeats of the fast and slow-formed cells. For fast-formed cells, most of the first-cycle charge capacity was extracted during the 1 h CV hold.

figures.label: S11
figures.caption: Figure S11: Half-cell CE measurement for electrodes harvested from full cells: (a) and (b) show NMCs and Grs in the same electrolyte system. NMC CE is around 90%, and Gr CE is around 92.5%.

figures.label: S12
figures.caption: Figure S12: Rate capability tests for fast (CC1 and CC2 > 1C, protocol with sequence number 106) and slow-formed (CC1 and CC2 = C/20, baseline formation protocol) cells at C/20, 1C and 2C. The capacity difference between fast and slow formation only shows up at low discharge rates (C/20).

figures.label: S13
figures.caption: Figure S13: Comparing the SOC distribution for positive electrode (PE) and negative electrode (NE) when they are both at the delithiated state (full cell at 3 V for NE and full cell at 4.4 V for PE). We observe that the distribution for both is less than 1% in this dataset.

figures.label: S14
figures.caption: Figure S14: Comparing the SOC distribution for PE and NE when they are both at the lithiated state (full cell at 4.4 V for NE and full cell at 3 V for PE). We observe that the distribution for both can be as large as 8%, and fast-formed cells tend to have less lithiated PE and NE.

figures.label: S15
figures.caption: Figure S15: Representative differential voltage analysis results for slow (a) – (c) and fast- formed cells (d) – (f). From left to right, we have dV/dQ, dQ/dV and V-Q curves. All of the first-cycle fitting results have a root mean squared error below 6mV. The slow-formed cell is identified by sequence number 169, and the fast-formed cell by sequence number 106.

figures.label: S16
figures.caption: Figure S16: Comparing electrode utilization shifts using dV/dQ plots. (a) – (b) show results for slow-formed cells and (c) – (d) show results for fast-formed cells. The half cell voltage is vs Li/Li+. NMC of the fast-formed cell after formation avoids the kinetic limited region, and graphite at full cell top of charge (4.4 V) is also less lithiated by comparing (a) to (c). Especially when comparing (b) to (d), we can clearly see that at 3 V (when the cell is fully discharged), the PE of the fast-formed cell avoids a big part of the steep voltage change in dV/dQ. The peaks of the grey solid line (real full cell) and the dotted line (fitted full cells) are well aligned, demonstrating the accuracy of the fitting results.

figures.label: S17
figures.caption: Figure S17: Full-cell Li inventory (QLi) extracted from differential voltage analysis plotted against (a) first-cycle formation charge capacity and (b) PE SOC at full cell bottom of discharge (3 V). Blue represents data from fast-formed cells. Extra capacity extracted during formation first charge are used for side reactions as opposed to Li intercalation which is accompanied by a decrease in Li inventory. The reduced Li inventory shifts the electrode utilization.

figures.label: S18
figures.caption: Figure S18: Resistance (100% SOC, 10s, discharge) measured by HPPC plotted against Li inventory, showing that lower Li inventory does not result in higher resistance. The blue markers represent fast-formed cells.

figures.label: S19
figures.caption: Figure S19: Charge capacity for fast-formed cells during the first formation cycle as a function of temperature. A significant component of Qch during fast formation arises from Li plating. The decrease in Qch with increasing temperature is attributed to improved Li intercalation kinetics and transport properties in graphite that reduce the likelihood of Li plating. All box plots display the interquartile range with box limits at the 25th and 75th percentiles. Whiskers extend 1.5 times the interquartile range from these percentiles, and outliers are represented by circles.

figures.label: S20
figures.caption: Figure S20: Charge capacity for slow-formed cells (CC1 and CC2 ≤C/5) during the first formation cycle as a function of temperature. Unlike in the fast-formed cells’ case, we observe increasing formation Qch with increasing temperature, suggesting that no or minimal Li plating occurs in the slow-formed cells.

figures.label: S21
figures.caption: Figure S21: C/5 discharge capacity with 1 h CV hold at the end of formation as a function of temperature for fast formed cells.

figures.label: S22
figures.caption: Figure S22: Disassembled graphite electrode sheet from a fast-formed full cell after for- mation charge and the 1 h CV hold at 4.4 V. The full cell was formed with CC1 = 0.295 A and CC2 = 0.283 A.

figures.label: S23
figures.caption: Figure S23: Disassembled graphite electrode sheet from a slow-formed full cell after formation charge and the 1 h CV hold at 4.4 V. The full cell was formed with CC1 = 0.012 A and CC2 = 0.012 A.

figures.label: S24
figures.caption: Figure S24: There is a correlation between Coulombic efficiency (CE) and cycle life for cells formed below 55°C, since shifted electrode utilization (a lower Li inventory) is also a reflection of the CE. However, for cells formed at 55°C, the electrode utilization or CE varies only narrowly, so no correlation can be established between CE and cycle life.
